newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian farm minister searches for farm financing.
newsitem.headline: Russian farm minister searches for farm financing.

text.p: Russia's troubled agricultural sector needs to find extra funding this year, possibly in the form of credits from commercial banks, Agriculture Minister Viktor Khlystun told a ministry meeting on Tuesday.
He also told Reuters that 1997 grain imports would be "about the same as in 1996," when official figures put total imports at 5.1 million tonnes. He gave no outright estimate for 1997.
"This year, we are looking at changes to the credit system," Khlystun told the meeting of officials, who met to discuss the fate of the farm sector for this year.
He said Russia would introduce a system of monetary credits to farmers, to gradually replace barter arrangements. Farmers have criticised the latter system as inadequate.
Khlystun said the ministry would transfer 2.8 trillion roubles from the budget into a soft credit fund for farmers, but said the amount fell well short of the sector's needs for 1997.
"According to the most extreme estimates, credit financing for the agricultural sector this season will need to be at least 18 trillion roubles," he said.
To help make up the difference, he said, the ministry would consider arranging credit arrangements with commercial banks.
"But commercial banks are not willing to deal with us without guarantees from the Finance Ministry," he said, adding that such guarantees were not forthcoming.
Khlystun called on the government to support the agricultural sector, which has found the transition from a centrally-planned system to a market system particularly hard.
"We need government regulation of the agricultural market, and we need to stimulate investment in our sector," he said.
Economy Minister Yevgeny Yasin, speaking at the same meeting, agreed that the struggling farming sector needed a special system of cheap credits and government support.
The Agriculture Ministry said on Monday it targeted net grain production in 1997 at 70 million tonnes, little changed from 69.3 million tonnes produced in 1996.
If fulfilled, this level would represent the third poor harvest in a row.
